Appendix I Removing the modality gap
[id=A9.SS0.SSS0.Px1]
[id=A9.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1] We investigate two methods and two baselines for removing the modality gap between II and TT. We measure the modality gap using the difference in mean (DiM) and the Wasserstein distance 𝒲\mathcal{W}, and consider the performance in recall on LAION. We also include COCO and ImageNet to study the transferability of our methods on unseen data distributions, and on unseen tasks.
[id=A9.SS0.SSS0.Px2]
Notations.
[id=A9.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1] Let’s first recall some notations. Let II and TT denote image and text embeddings, with respective mean μI\mu_{I} and μT\mu_{T}. Let ZIZ_{I}, ZTZ_{T} be the codes of II, TT given by our SAE. Let DD be the dictionary, and 𝜹∈{0,1}K\bm{\delta}\in\{0,1\}^{K} be the binary mask selecting bimodal features, and broadcasted to the size of the codes.
Let I^≔ZI​D\widehat{I}\coloneqq Z_{I}D be the set of reconstructed activations, and I~≔(ZI⊙𝜹)​D\widetilde{I}\coloneqq(Z_{I}\odot\bm{\delta})D, and similarly for T^\widehat{T} and T~\widetilde{T}.
[id=A9.SS0.SSS0.Px3]
[id=A9.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1] Our first method comes from the analysis of our SAEs : we remove unimodal concepts, ending up with I~\widetilde{I} and T~\widetilde{T}. This is the only method that doesn’t enforce the mean of the two distribution to exactly match. Instead, we rely on our SAEs to capture all shared representations. As a baseline we propose to consider the centered versions of the data Icenter≔I^−𝝁𝑰^I_{\mathrm{center}}\coloneqq\widehat{I}-\bm{\mu_{\widehat{I}}} and Tcenter≔T^−𝝁𝑻^T_{\mathrm{center}}\coloneqq\widehat{T}-\bm{\mu_{\widehat{T}}}. The motivation for this baseline is the observation in Appendix F that unimodal features are predominantly small variations around a unique direction, except for small energy ones which are orders of magnitude less energetic.
[id=A9.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.1] For the above baseline and the next two methods, we use reconstructed embeddings instead of the original ones for fairness of comparison, as SAEs never perfectly reconstruct activations. Additionally, for the means, we use the means on the LAION dataset even on COCO and on ImageNet, also for fairness, as SAEs were trained on the LAION dataset.
[id=A9.SS0.SSS0.Px4]
[id=A9.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1] The second method is called embedding shift in Liang et al. (2022), and it essentially consist in the following transformation : Ishift≔I^−𝝁𝑰^+𝝁𝑰^+𝝁𝑻^𝟐I_{\mathrm{shift}}\coloneqq\widehat{I}-\bm{\mu_{\widehat{I}}}+\bm{\frac{\mu_{\widehat{I}}+\mu_{\widehat{T}}}{2}} and Tshift≔T^−𝝁𝑻^+𝝁𝑰^+𝝁𝑻^𝟐T_{\mathrm{shift}}\coloneqq\widehat{T}-\bm{\mu_{\widehat{T}}}+\bm{\frac{\mu_{\widehat{I}}+\mu_{\widehat{T}}}{2}}. We propose the following baseline for this method : we replace the average of the means by a random direction 𝒓\bm{r}, sampled uniformly from the unit sphere—Irand≔I^−𝝁𝑰^+𝒓I_{\mathrm{rand}}\coloneqq\widehat{I}-\bm{\mu_{\widehat{I}}}+\bm{r} and Trand≔T^−𝝁𝑻^+𝒓T_{\mathrm{rand}}\coloneqq\widehat{T}-\bm{\mu_{\widehat{T}}}+\bm{r}.
[id=A9.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p2.1] These two methods are not comparable to the first two in terms of modality gap, as even if the DiM is similar, the Wasserstein distance 𝒲\mathcal{W} behaves very differently. Indeed, in the first two methods, data is centered around 00 and is roughly uniformly spread on the unit sphere. On the other hand, by manually adding a mean, these methods concentrate the data on a narrow cone, significantly reducing the 𝒲\mathcal{W}. We illustrate these four methods on synthetic 3D points in Figure 24.
Figure 24: Illustration of the four methods to remove the modality gap on synthetic data points.
[id=A9.SS0.SSS0.Px5]
[id=A9.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.1] Results are compiled in Tables 9, 10 and 11. We can see that the shift method introduced in previous work is by far the worst, significantly reducing recall performances, then comes the random baseline. The mean baseline outperforms the concept-based approach in terms of recall, but it does not close the modality gap.
[id=A9.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p2.1] We also indicate in Figure 25 the KNN distance histograms for our four methods, following the OOD detection method described in Appendix H, for the CLIP-L model on the LAION dataset. We take the image distribution as the reference one, and the text distribution as the ”OOD” one. This illustrates a bit more precisely the effect of all methods on the distribution of embeddings. We can see that our method is the only one that closes the gap by merging the two distributions.
Figure 25: Histogram of distances from each image (ID) and caption (OOD) embedding to it’s 10th nearest neighbor in the corresponding distribution of image embeddings. We use CLIP-L and the LAION dataset. As explained in Appendix I, the shift method and our concept based method can’t be compared in terms of distances, they can only be compared to their respective baselines. Indeed, distances in the random baseline and shift method are artificially small, but we can see from these histograms that the two distributions can still be very well separated. They are however comparable in histogram separation and recall, which we indicate. Our concept based method is the only one to truly close the gap by matching the image and text distribution.

Table 9: Recall performance and modality gap in LAION’s reconstructed embeddings, after the shift method and our concept based method to remove the gap, and after two baselines adapted to each method. As explained in Appendix I, the modality gap between the shift and concept based methods are not comparable, they can only be compared to their respective baselines. We can see that the shift method performs by far the worst in terms of recall. The concept based method seems to be consistently worse in terms of recall than it’s baseline in terms of recall on smaller models, and equivalent in larger ones. However, in terms of modality gap, it is much better, with the mean baseline closing the gap in DiM but leaving it almost untouched in terms of distribution (𝒲\mathcal{W}).

Appendix J Datasets
[id=A10.p1.1] Throughout this study, we used four datasets : LAION-400M (Schuhmann et al., 2021), COCO (Lin et al., 2014), ImageNet (Deng et al., 2009) and FashionIQ (Wu et al., 2021).
[id=A10.SS0.SSS0.Px1]
LAION.
[id=A10.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1] We randomly selected a subset of 1M image-caption samples from the LAION-400M dataset. These samples were used to generate matching image-text embeddings. All reported SAEs were trained on this dataset.

COCO.

Appendix J Datasets
[id=A10.p1.1] Throughout this study, we used four datasets : LAION-400M (Schuhmann et al., 2021), COCO (Lin et al., 2014), ImageNet (Deng et al., 2009) and FashionIQ (Wu et al., 2021).
[id=A10.SS0.SSS0.Px1]
LAION.
[id=A10.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1] We randomly selected a subset of 1M image-caption samples from the LAION-400M dataset. These samples were used to generate matching image-text embeddings. All reported SAEs were trained on this dataset.
[id=A10.SS0.SSS0.Px2]
COCO.
[id=A10.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1] We used the train split of the 2017 update of the COCO dataset. Each image being paired with multiple captions, we generated pairs by duplicating the images for each of their captions. This dataset was used to further test the VLM encoders as well as the transferability of the learned features.
[id=A10.SS0.SSS0.Px3]
ImageNet.
[id=A10.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1] This dataset was used to study the transferability of our features on a downstream classification task, commonly used in the literature. We generated about 80 captions for each class, embedded them, and averaged each class’s embeddings to get a linear classifier, following Radford et al. (2021)’s method.
Figure 26: Examples of image-caption pairs in the LAION (top), COCO (center) and ImageNet (bottom).
[id=A10.SS0.SSS0.Px4]
FashionIQ.
[id=A10.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1] This dataset is used to evaluate retrieval performance. It contains source images, called candidate, target images, and relative captions capturing the difference between the candidate and target. When several relative captions are available for a single candidate-target pair, we proceed as in ImageNet: we embed each caption and mean the results.
Figure 27: Examples of source and target images in FashionIQ, along with their relative caption.
[id=A11]
Appendix K Why remove bias before comparing content
[id=A11.p1.1] One could ask why it is important to remove unimodal information and what impact this has on retrieval and other downstream tasks. Can it help improve performance by cleaning the representation and revealing the useful semantic information? Building on the fact that many works have found that modality-specific components live in orthogonal subspaces, we are left with two choices: either the modality information acts as a constant offset, in which case removing or adding it does not change rankings, or the modality information is adaptive, as we find in this work. In the adaptive case, retrieval rankings can change significantly, making our decomposition a useful tool for precise control and steering of retrieval systems.
We detail this here, and start with our setup.
[id=A11.SS0.SSS0.Px1]
Setup
[id=A11.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1] We work in a representation space ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} that decomposes orthogonally as ℝd=Γ⊕Ω\mathbb{R}^{d}=\Gamma\oplus\Omega into a content subspace Γ\Gamma and a modality subspace Ω\Omega with Γ⟂Ω\Gamma\perp\Omega. For any underlying item 𝒙\bm{x}, the observed embedding factorizes as
[id=A11.Ex4]
𝒗=𝝎⁡(𝒙)⏟modality ∈Ω+𝜸⁡(𝒙)⏟content ∈Γwithℝd=Γ⊕Ω\bm{v}=\underbrace{\bm{\omega}(\bm{x})}_{\text{modality }\in\Omega}+\underbrace{\bm{\gamma}(\bm{x})}_{\text{content }\in\Gamma}\quad\text{with}\quad\mathbb{R}^{d}=\Gamma\oplus\Omega
[id=A11.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.2] where 𝝎⁡(𝒙)∈Ω\bm{\omega}(\bm{x})\in\Omega captures modality-specific information and 𝜸⁡(𝒙)∈Γ\bm{\gamma}(\bm{x})\in\Gamma represents the semantic content estimated by our SAE. The orthogonal direct sum decomposition ensures that content and modality components are geometrically independent.
[id=A11.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.1] For retrieval, we score against a set of unit-normalized candidates {𝒚i}i=1n\{\bm{y}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n} using cosine similarity. To analyze pairwise rankings, we define the content margin Δc​(i,j)≔⟨𝜸⁡(𝒙),𝒚i−𝒚j⟩\Delta_{c}(i,j)\coloneqq\langle\bm{\gamma}(\bm{x}),\bm{y}_{i}-\bm{y}_{j}\rangle and the modality margin Δm​(i,j)≔⟨𝝎⁡(𝒙),𝒚i−𝒚j⟩\Delta_{m}(i,j)\coloneqq\langle\bm{\omega}(\bm{x}),\bm{y}_{i}-\bm{y}_{j}\rangle. We also write αi≔⟨𝝎⁡(𝒙),𝒚i⟩\alpha_{i}\coloneqq\langle\bm{\omega}(\bm{x}),\bm{y}_{i}\rangle for the modality projection onto candidate ii.
[id=A11.SS1]
K.1 Constant modality information
[id=A11.SS1.p1.1] We first consider the case where modality information affects all candidates equally. This corresponds to the intuitive scenario where modality acts as a simple offset that shifts all similarities by the same amount, leaving relative rankings unchanged.
[id=A11.SS1.p2.1] When the modality component 𝝎⁡(𝒙)\bm{\omega}(\bm{x}) projects with identical strength onto every candidate in the retrieval set, removing this component preserves all pairwise orderings. This formalizes the intuition that a candidate-independent offset cannot affect relative rankings.
Proposition 2 (Ranking invariance under constant projection).
[id=Thmproposition2.p1.1] Assume unit normalized candidates {𝐲i}i=1n\{\bm{y}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}. If there exists α∈ℝ\alpha\in\mathbb{R} such that ⟨𝛚⁡(𝐱),𝐲i⟩=α\langle\bm{\omega}(\bm{x}),\bm{y}_{i}\rangle=\alpha for all ii, then for any ii and jj
[id=A11.Ex5]
cos(𝒗,𝒚i)>cos(𝒗,𝒚j)⇔cos(𝜸(𝒙),𝒚i)>cos(𝜸(𝒙),𝒚j)\cos(\bm{v},\bm{y}_{i})>\cos(\bm{v},\bm{y}_{j})\quad\iff\quad\cos(\bm{\gamma}(\bm{x}),\bm{y}_{i})>\cos(\bm{\gamma}(\bm{x}),\bm{y}_{j})
[id=Thmproposition2.p1.2] The same equivalence holds with equality. The statement also holds for dot product scoring.
Proof.
[id=A11.SS1.p3.1] With ‖𝒚i‖=1\|\bm{y}_{i}\|=1 we have
[id=A11.Ex6]
cos⁡(𝒗,𝒚i)=⟨𝒗,𝒚i⟩‖𝒗‖=⟨𝝎⁡(𝒙),𝒚i⟩+⟨𝜸⁡(𝒙),𝒚i⟩‖𝒗‖\cos(\bm{v},\bm{y}_{i})=\frac{\langle\bm{v},\bm{y}_{i}\rangle}{\|\bm{v}\|}=\frac{\langle\bm{\omega}(\bm{x}),\bm{y}_{i}\rangle+\langle\bm{\gamma}(\bm{x}),\bm{y}_{i}\rangle}{\|\bm{v}\|}

[id=A11.SS1.p7.1] In the constant modality regime, removing modality information yields only the subspace of interest, and potentially more interpretable multimodal embeddings, but without any performance gains or losses.
Thus, in that case, the decomposition provides the content representation by eliminating modality-specific artifacts, but since rankings remain identical, one should not expect improvements in retrieval metrics. This case represents a neutral scenario where the primary benefit is representational clarity rather than functional enhancement.
[id=A11.SS1.p8.1] We now consider a near-constant case where modality projections vary slightly across candidates. This provides a useful practical criterion for when small variations cannot disrupt content-based rankings.

[id=A11.SS1.p11.1] This corollary establishes a robustness condition: when modality variations are small relative to content differences—even in the presence of multiple adaptive modality components – the content signal prevails and rankings remain unchanged. Like the constant case, decomposition offers no performance gains here since content already drives the original rankings.
[id=A11.SS1.p12.1] However, as we will show next and as we empirically find in this work, real modality information is typically adaptive rather than constant, leading to significant ranking changes when removed.

K.2 Adaptive modality information
[id=A11.SS2.p1.1] This is what we observe empirically in this work. The modality signal decomposes into multiple unimodal atoms and the modality projection varies significantly across candidates. In this regime, removing 𝝎⁡(𝒙)\bm{\omega}(\bm{x}) can dramatically change rankings. The next proposition provides a necessary and sufficient condition for ranking flips and clarifies that flips occur when the candidate-dependent modality margin opposes and dominates the content margin.
